- When sentiment is high (≥0.7) and forecast is significantly above recent history, reduce forecast by 5–15% to avoid over-optimism.  
- If forecast peaks sharply after a recent spike and sentiment is neutral or declining, apply a downward correction of 5–10% to prevent overshoot.  
- When true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days falling below 70), adjust forecast to reflect downward bias, especially if sentiment is low (<0.5).  
- If forecast is consistently 5–10% above true outcome over 3–5 days, apply a “lag correction” — reduce forecast by 2–5% for the next 3–5 days to account for delayed reaction.  
- For horizon > 14 days, reduce forecast sensitivity to sentiment swings — use sentiment as a multiplier (e.g., 0.8–0.9) to dampen overreaction.  
- If sentiment is high but true outcome is low (e.g., >0.7 but price drops), assume sentiment is misaligned — reduce forecast by 10–20% to correct for sentiment-driven overvaluation.
